solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Magician on island, rich, having abandoned US (8)

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so the US drops out

blocks.note: prosperous = rich
used literally; these are the letters removed

annotation.surface: A wealthy conjuror who has turned his back on America.
annotation.walkthrough: PROSPERO is the magician marooned on an island in Shakespeare's The Tempest, and 'US' is just the two letters, not the country.
annotation.definitionFit: Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, practises magic on the island where The Tempest is set.

entries.clue: Theorem musician holds up part of year (6)

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer inside it
in a down clue, 'up' means read the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters theo-REM MUS-ician, run together

annotation.surface: A musician who is also a mathematician is tied to a proof and stalls a piece of the calendar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Theorem' tempts you towards SUM, which is a false start: the answer sits across the join of the two words and runs backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by category: the warm season is one of the four quarters the year divides into.

entries.clue: Noble quality of larch, wound round with ivy (8)

indicators.note: letters that are wound round are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: used literally
used literally; 'with' joins the two parts of the fodder

annotation.surface: A larch tree with ivy twined round its trunk, somehow displaying nobility.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wound' is not an injury here but the past tense of wind, as ivy winds round a tree.
annotation.definitionFit: Chivalry is the courteous, honourable conduct of an ideal knight, a noble quality.

entries.clue: Good group of students: they’re native to Africa (4)

blocks.note: G = good
the NUS is the National Union of Students

annotation.surface: A well-behaved student group turns out to be from Africa.
annotation.walkthrough: The NUS is the UK's National Union of Students. The colon hides the switch from students to animals.
annotation.definitionFit: Gnus, or wildebeest, are antelopes found only in Africa.

entries.clue: Stop draft (4,2)

blocks.note: a car draws up when it pulls in and stops
to prepare a document in written form; the same phrasal verb covers both senses

annotation.walkthrough: Both words read as verbs: a vehicle draws up at the kerb, and a lawyer draws up a contract.
annotation.definitionFit: To draw up is both to come to a halt and to compose a written draft.

entries.clue: Oral exclamation of support (4)

blocks.note: a noun here: a spoken university examination
a cheer meaning 'long live!', borrowed from Italian and Spanish

annotation.surface: A spoken cheer of encouragement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oral' is a noun here: in British universities a viva (viva voce) is an oral examination.
annotation.definitionFit: Viva is both an oral exam and a cry of 'long live!'

entries.clue: Somewhat absurd, using this language (4)

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, part of the phrase

blocks.note: the last three letters of absurd plus the first of using

annotation.surface: Someone complains that speaking this tongue is a bit ridiculous.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma does not stop the run of letters: the answer straddles it.
annotation.definitionFit: Urdu is a language, official in Pakistan and widely spoken in India.

entries.clue: Give wading bird protection on flight? (8)

blocks.note: to hand something over is to give it
a rail is a marsh bird

annotation.surface: Handing a wading bird over as a safeguard for an air journey.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flight' suggests aeroplanes, especially next to a bird; it is a flight of stairs, and the question mark flags the twist.
annotation.definitionFit: A handrail keeps you safe on a flight of stairs.

entries.clue: US writer’s visa returned, opened by medic (6)

definitions.note: the definition is possessive, but the 's belongs to the surface; the answer is the writer

indicators.note: sent back, so the letters run the other way
the medic is let in, splitting the word open

blocks.note: used literally
MO = medical officer

annotation.surface: An American author's travel papers are handed back and checked by a doctor.
annotation.walkthrough: Isaac Asimov was the American science-fiction writer. MO, medical officer, is a common crossword doctor.
annotation.definitionFit: Isaac Asimov was a prolific American writer, best known for his science fiction.

entries.clue: Headgear for pig? It’s of no consequence (2,4)

blocks.note: a sow is a female pig
a hat is headgear

annotation.surface: A comic image of a pig in a hat, dismissed with a shrug.
annotation.walkthrough: A hat for a sow is a SOW HAT; respaced, it becomes the shrug SO WHAT.
annotation.definitionFit: 'So what?' dismisses something as unimportant, of no consequence.

entries.clue: Pick up present for audience (4)

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: present = here, as when answering a register

annotation.surface: Collecting a gift meant for the spectators.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift; it is the adjective, as in 'present and correct', meaning here.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: you 'pick up' a sound or a rumour when it reaches your ears.

entries.clue: Someone entitled to organise rep, I feel? (4,4)

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: used literally

annotation.surface: Someone with a sense of entitlement musing that they ought to arrange the sales rep's affairs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Entitled' reads as spoilt or presumptuous; here it means holding a title. A life peer is a British lord whose title is not inherited.
annotation.definitionFit: A life peer is given a title and a seat in the House of Lords for life.

entries.clue: Do top of face with ointment (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of face
unction is an ointment or anointing oil

annotation.surface: An instruction to put cream on your forehead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do' is a noun: a do is a party, just as a function is a formal gathering.
annotation.definitionFit: A function is a social event or party, which is what a do is.

entries.clue: Australian bird the French boy copied (8)

blocks.note: the emu is a large flightless Australian bird
la = the, in French (feminine)
Ted is a boy's name

annotation.surface: A French lad imitated the Australian bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The French' is either LE or LA; here it has to be LA.
annotation.definitionFit: To emulate someone is to copy them in the hope of matching them.

entries.clue: Use sparingly any goose that’s been cooked (2,4,2)

indicators.note: to cook the books is to falsify them, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: used literally

annotation.surface: Advice to be frugal with leftover roast goose.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture makes 'cooked' natural; its job is to scramble the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to go easy on the butter is to ration it, using less than you might.

entries.clue: Ottoman commander with short Thai girl (6)

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: an aga was a Turkish military commander
THAI loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A Turkish officer escorting a petite girl from Thailand.
annotation.walkthrough: AGA, the Ottoman commander, turns up often in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Agatha is one girl's name among many, as in Agatha Christie.

entries.clue: Dry and dreary routine linked to bachelor (4)

indicators.note: the two parts are joined together

blocks.note: B = bachelor, as in degrees like BA
to be in a rut is to be stuck in a dull routine

annotation.surface: A single man's life described as dull and monotonous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dry' looks like part of the dull description; it defines the answer, in its wine sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Brut describes very dry champagne or sparkling wine.

entries.clue: Pupil once turning eleven, no good for sport (6)

indicators.note: turned round, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: an OB is an old boy, a former pupil
XI = eleven, in Roman numerals and as a sports team
NG = no good

annotation.surface: A former pupil turns out for the eleven but proves useless at the game.
annotation.walkthrough: An old boy is a former pupil of a British school. 'Eleven' suggests a football or cricket side, which is why it becomes XI.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: boxing is one sport among many, fought with gloved fists in a ring.

entries.clue: Quietly furious one’s stealing from work (6)

definitions.note: 'one's' is 'one is': the definition is a clause describing the pirate

blocks.note: p = piano, quietly in music
irate = furious

annotation.surface: An employee silently fuming about someone pilfering from the office.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work' is not the workplace but a creative work: a pirate copies books, films or music illegally.
annotation.definitionFit: A pirate illegally copies and sells someone else's creative work.

entries.clue: Wader I put on twice (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, I is put on top of the next piece

blocks.note: used literally
bis = twice, the Latin word used on scores for a repeat

annotation.surface: Someone who dresses twice over.
annotation.walkthrough: BIS is Latin for twice and appears in music and in street numbers such as 12 bis.
annotation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-legged wading bird.

entries.clue: Arriving in good time – not quite 12? (4)

definitions.note: the definition is a cross-reference: 12 across is LIFE PEER, and an earl is one kind of peer

indicators.note: the word falls just short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: early = arriving in good time

annotation.surface: Getting somewhere just before noon.
annotation.walkthrough: '12' looks like a clock time; it points to 12 across, LIFE PEER. An earl is a peer, though usually by inheritance, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: An earl is a member of the peerage, as a life peer is.

entries.clue: Cross parent coming in to beat government official? (6)

blocks.note: X is a cross
ma = mother
to tan someone's hide is to beat them

annotation.surface: An angry parent barging in to thump a bureaucrat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry beside 'parent'; it is the letter X. The question mark admits a taxman is not strictly an official title.
annotation.definitionFit: The taxman collects taxes on behalf of the government.

entries.clue: Thro’ it, he flourished, previously (8)

indicators.note: letters that are flourished are waved about into a new order

blocks.note: used literally; thro’ is an old spelling of through

annotation.surface: An old-fashioned line: through it, he prospered in times past.
annotation.walkthrough: The archaic 'thro'' suits the old-fashioned answer and supplies exactly the letters needed.
annotation.definitionFit: Hitherto means until now, previously.

entries.clue: Trotsky maybe has returned for Christmas (4)

indicators.note: come back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: Leon Trotsky, the Russian revolutionary; 'maybe' marks him as one Leon among many

annotation.surface: The exiled revolutionary is back home for the holidays.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trotsky maybe' is a definition by example: he stands for any Leon.
annotation.definitionFit: Noel is a word for Christmas, as in the carol 'The First Nowell'.
